SPAR POSTOPERATIVE HANDOVER

Patient: 50-year-old patient
Diagnosis: Lumbar discitis at L3–L4 and L4–L5
Procedure: L3–L4 and L4–L5 discectomy for discitis

S — Situation

A 50-year-old patient with lumbar discitis involving the L3–L4 and L4–L5 intervertebral disc spaces underwent discectomy at both levels.

The patient is currently stable on postoperative day 1. Current observations are: blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, heart rate 82 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, temperature 37.2°C, and pain score 4/10 after analgesia.

The patient requires continued postoperative monitoring, neurological assessment, pain management, wound care, and treatment and surveillance of the underlying spinal infection.

P — Patient Background

The patient was diagnosed with lumbar discitis involving L3–L4 and L4–L5 and underwent surgical intervention.

* Past medical history: Hypertension for 5 years, controlled with amlodipine 5 mg once daily; no history of diabetes mellitus, tuberculosis, or immunosuppression.
* Past surgical history: No previous spinal surgery; laparoscopic appendicectomy 12 years ago.
* Allergies: No known drug allergies.
* Preoperative symptoms: 6-week history of severe lower-back pain rated 8/10, worse with movement, associated with bilateral thigh pain and difficulty walking. No preoperative bowel or bladder dysfunction was reported.
* Preoperative neurological examination: Lower-limb power was 5/5 bilaterally, sensation was intact, and reflexes were symmetrical. The patient mobilised with an antalgic gait because of pain.
* Imaging: MRI of the lumbar spine demonstrated inflammatory changes and disc-space involvement at L3–L4 and L4–L5, with adjacent end-plate changes and no significant epidural abscess.
* Operative procedure: L3–L4 and L4–L5 discectomy with removal of infected disc material and collection of intraoperative tissue samples.
* Estimated blood loss: 150 mL.
* Intraoperative complications: None reported.
* Drain: One closed-suction drain inserted at the operative site.
* Infection workup: Two sets of blood cultures were collected preoperatively. Intraoperative disc and tissue samples were sent for microscopy, culture, sensitivity, and histopathology.
* Antimicrobial treatment: Intravenous vancomycin 1 g every 12 hours and ceftriaxone 2 g once daily were commenced pending culture results, with renal-dose adjustment and infectious-disease review planned.

A — Assessment

General condition

* General condition: Awake, alert, cooperative, and haemodynamically stable.
* Airway and breathing: Airway patent; breathing unlaboured; bilateral air entry equal; no respiratory distress.
* Blood pressure: 128/76 mmHg.
* Heart rate: 82 beats/min, regular.
* Respiratory rate: 18 breaths/min.
* Oxygen saturation: 98% on room air.
* Temperature: 37.2°C.
* Pain: 4/10 at rest and 6/10 on movement; partially relieved by prescribed analgesia.
* Fluid balance: Intake 1,800 mL and urine output 1,200 mL over the last 24 hours.
* Urine output: Approximately 50 mL/hour; patient voiding spontaneously.

Neurological examination

* Glasgow Coma Scale: 15/15: E4, V5, M6.
* Higher functions: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time; speech clear; no confusion.
* Lower-limb motor power:
    * Hip flexion: right 5/5, left 5/5.
    * Knee extension: right 5/5, left 5/5.
    * Ankle dorsiflexion: right 5/5, left 5/5.
    * Great-toe extension: right 5/5, left 5/5.
    * Ankle plantarflexion: right 5/5, left 5/5.
* Sensory examination: Light touch and pinprick sensation intact in both lower limbs; no new dermatomal sensory loss.
* Lower-limb reflexes: Patellar reflexes 2+ bilaterally; Achilles reflexes 2+ bilaterally; plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
* Saddle sensation: Intact bilaterally.
* Sphincter function: No urinary retention or incontinence; no bowel incontinence; patient passed urine spontaneously.
* Mobility: Mobilised 10 metres with a walking frame and one-person assistance.
* Comparison with preoperative baseline: Neurological examination remains unchanged from baseline, with preserved power and sensation bilaterally.

Surgical site

* Dressing: Clean, dry, and intact.
* Wound: No active bleeding, erythema, wound separation, or purulent discharge.
* Swelling: Mild expected postoperative local swelling; no expanding collection.
* Drain: One closed-suction drain in situ; 60 mL of serosanguineous output over the last 24 hours; no frank blood or purulent material.
* Drain site: Clean and secure.

Postoperative investigations

* Haemoglobin: 11.8 g/dL, decreased from 13.2 g/dL preoperatively.
* White-cell count: 12.4 × 10⁹/L.
* Platelet count: 286 × 10⁹/L.
* C-reactive protein: 86 mg/L.
* Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 58 mm/hour.
* Creatinine: 92 µmol/L.
* Urea: 6.8 mmol/L.
* Sodium: 138 mmol/L.
* Potassium: 4.2 mmol/L.
* Blood cultures: No growth at 24 hours; final result pending.
* Intraoperative cultures: Disc and tissue cultures pending.
* Histopathology: Pending.
* Postoperative imaging: Lumbar spine radiographs requested to assess alignment and exclude an unexpected postoperative complication; no urgent imaging indication currently identified.

Clinical impression

A 50-year-old patient on postoperative day 1 following L3–L4 and L4–L5 discectomy for lumbar discitis. The patient is haemodynamically stable, neurologically intact with bilateral lower-limb power of 5/5, and has a clean surgical wound. Mild postoperative anaemia and inflammatory-marker elevation are present. The drain is functioning with low-volume serosanguineous output. Ongoing priorities are neurological surveillance, wound and drain care, pain control, mobilisation, and targeted antimicrobial treatment once culture results are available.

R — Recommendation

1. Continue postoperative observations every 4 hours, including blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, pain score, and level of consciousness.
2. Perform neurological observations every 4 hours, documenting bilateral lower-limb motor power, sensation, reflexes, saddle sensation, and bladder and bowel function.
3. Continue prescribed analgesia: paracetamol 1 g orally every 6 hours, with opioid analgesia as required for breakthrough pain; reassess pain within 60 minutes of administration.
4. Continue intravenous vancomycin 1 g every 12 hours and ceftriaxone 2 g once daily pending microbiology results; monitor vancomycin levels and renal function.
5. Review blood cultures, intraoperative cultures, and histopathology when available, and narrow or modify antibiotics in consultation with infectious-disease specialists.
6. Monitor the wound and dressing at least once per shift for bleeding, erythema, swelling, wound separation, or purulent discharge.
7. Measure and document drain output every 8 hours; notify the surgical team if output exceeds 100 mL in 8 hours, becomes bright red, becomes purulent, or increases unexpectedly.
8. Repeat complete blood count, renal function, C-reactive protein, and electrolytes in 24 hours or earlier if the patient deteriorates.
9. Maintain strict fluid balance and monitor urine output, aiming for at least 0.5 mL/kg/hour.
10. Encourage mobilisation with physiotherapy three times daily as tolerated, using a walking frame and spinal precautions as directed by the operating surgeon.
11. Provide venous-thromboembolism prevention with intermittent pneumatic compression and pharmacological prophylaxis when approved by the surgical team.
12. Maintain a regular diet as tolerated and encourage adequate protein and fluid intake to support wound healing.
13. Arrange infectious-disease review within 24 hours to determine the duration and route of antimicrobial therapy.
14. Arrange neurosurgical review within 24 hours and confirm the timing of drain removal and follow-up imaging.
15. Escalate urgently for new or worsening lower-limb weakness, sensory loss, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention, urinary or faecal incontinence, severe uncontrolled pain, rapidly increasing wound swelling, purulent discharge, fever above 38.0°C with clinical deterioration, hypotension, tachycardia, or reduced level of consciousness.
16. Before discharge, confirm a documented antimicrobial plan, wound-care instructions, mobilisation and rehabilitation plan, follow-up appointments, repeat inflammatory-marker monitoring, and clear return precautions.

Patient: 50-year-old patient
Procedure: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion with internal fixation at C5–C6

S — Situation

A 50-year-old patient is postoperative day 0 following an uncomplicated anterior cervical discectomy and fusion at C5–C6 for cervical disc prolapse with spinal cord and nerve-root compression. The patient is awake, haemodynamically stable, and neurologically intact compared with the preoperative baseline.

Current priorities are continued neurological observation, airway and swallowing assessment, pain management, wound monitoring, and early mobilisation as directed by the neurosurgical team.

Current vital signs: Blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, heart rate 82 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C.
Immediate concerns: Monitor for new limb weakness or sensory loss, airway compromise, neck swelling or haematoma, dysphagia, voice changes, uncontrolled pain, wound bleeding, and postoperative infection.

P — Patient Background

* Age: 50 years.
* Primary diagnosis: C5–C6 cervical disc prolapse causing cervical radiculopathy and early myelopathic symptoms.
* Procedure performed: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion with insertion of an interbody cage, anterior plate, and screws at C5–C6.
* Operated level: C5–C6.
* Indication: Persistent neck pain and right upper-limb radicular pain with progressive hand numbness and reduced grip strength despite conservative treatment.
* Presenting symptoms: Six-month history of neck pain radiating to the right shoulder and arm, paraesthesia affecting the thumb and index finger, and difficulty with fine hand movements. No preoperative bowel or bladder dysfunction.
* Relevant medical history: Hypertension controlled with amlodipine 5 mg once daily. No diabetes, cardiac disease, or previous spinal surgery. No known drug allergies. The patient was not taking anticoagulants or antiplatelet medication.
* Preoperative neurological status: Alert and oriented. Right hand grip 4+/5, right wrist extension 4+/5, and remaining upper- and lower-limb muscle groups 5/5. Mildly reduced sensation in the right C6 dermatome. Gait was independent. No bowel or bladder disturbance.
* Imaging: MRI demonstrated a C5–C6 posterolateral disc protrusion with foraminal narrowing and mild anterior indentation of the spinal cord, greater on the right side. No significant cord signal change was reported.
* Intraoperative course: Procedure completed under general anaesthesia without reported complications. Intraoperative neuromonitoring remained stable. Estimated blood loss was approximately 50 mL. No dural tear or cerebrospinal fluid leak was reported.
* Implant: Interbody cage packed with bone graft, anterior cervical plate, and four fixation screws at C5–C6. Implant position was satisfactory on intraoperative imaging.
* Drain: One small closed-suction drain placed in the anterior neck wound, with minimal serosanguineous output.
* Postoperative plan: Continue neurological and airway observations, maintain the wound dressing, monitor drain output, provide multimodal analgesia, mobilise with assistance when fully awake, and obtain postoperative cervical spine radiographs as requested by the surgeon.

A — Assessment

1. General condition

* General appearance and level of consciousness: Awake, alert, calm, and responding appropriately. No acute distress.
* GCS: 15/15.
* Blood pressure: 132/78 mmHg.
* Heart rate: 82 beats/min.
* Respiratory rate: 16 breaths/min.
* Oxygen saturation: 98% on room air.
* Temperature: 36.7 °C.
* Pain score: 4/10 at the anterior neck incision.
* Pain control: Adequate after prescribed intravenous analgesia. No severe radicular pain reported.

2. Neurological assessment

* Right upper-limb motor power: Shoulder abduction 5/5, elbow flexion 5/5, elbow extension 5/5, wrist extension 5/5, wrist flexion 5/5, finger abduction 5/5, and hand grip 5/5.
* Left upper-limb motor power: Shoulder abduction 5/5, elbow flexion 5/5, elbow extension 5/5, wrist extension 5/5, wrist flexion 5/5, finger abduction 5/5, and hand grip 5/5.
* Lower-limb motor power: Bilateral hip flexion, knee extension, ankle dorsiflexion, great-toe extension, and plantarflexion 5/5.
* Sensory examination: Sensation intact in all four limbs. The preoperative right C6 paraesthesia has improved. No new numbness or saddle sensory disturbance.
* Reflexes: Biceps, triceps, and brachioradialis reflexes present and symmetrical. No new pathological reflexes identified.
* Gait and mobility: Not yet fully assessed because the patient is immediately postoperative; able to move all limbs independently in bed. Mobilisation will be assessed once fully recovered from anaesthesia.
* Bladder and bowel function: No preoperative dysfunction. Patient has not yet voided postoperatively; monitor urine output and assess for urinary retention.
* Comparison with preoperative baseline: Motor function is improved to 5/5 in the previously weak right hand. Sensory symptoms are reduced. No new neurological deficit identified.

3. Surgical site and procedure-specific assessment

* Wound: Anterior neck dressing clean, dry, and intact. No active bleeding, expanding swelling, erythema, or discharge.
* Drain: Closed-suction drain patent with approximately 10 mL of serosanguineous output since arrival in recovery. No sudden increase in output.
* Pain: Mild incisional neck pain rated 4/10. No recurrent right arm pain or new radicular symptoms.
* Airway and swallowing: Breathing comfortably on room air. Voice clear. No stridor, respiratory distress, neck tightness, or rapidly increasing swelling. Mild discomfort on swallowing but able to swallow water without coughing or choking.
* Fluid balance: Intravenous fluids ongoing as prescribed. Urine output to be monitored; target is at least 0.5 mL/kg/hour.
* Mobilisation: Bed rest until fully awake, followed by assisted sitting and mobilisation with nursing or physiotherapy support. Avoid sudden neck movements and heavy lifting.

4. Investigations and postoperative review

* Preoperative haemoglobin was 13.8 g/dL, white-cell count 7.4 × 10⁹/L, platelets 248 × 10⁹/L, and creatinine 82 µmol/L.
* Postoperative blood tests are planned for the following morning unless clinically indicated earlier.
* Postoperative cervical spine radiographs are requested to confirm alignment and implant position.
* The operative report confirms satisfactory decompression and stable fixation.
* Continue to review drain output, wound appearance, neurological findings, swallowing, and airway status.

5. Clinical impression

A 50-year-old patient is stable on the day of surgery following uncomplicated C5–C6 anterior cervical discectomy and fusion with internal fixation. The patient is alert, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably, and has no new neurological deficit. Preoperative right-hand weakness and C6 sensory symptoms have improved. The wound is clean and the drain has minimal serosanguineous output. Continued monitoring is required for postoperative neurological deterioration, airway compromise, neck haematoma, dysphagia, infection, and pain.

R — Recommendation

1. Continue vital-sign monitoring and postoperative observations according to the neurosurgical unit protocol.
2. Perform neurological observations hourly initially, including GCS, pupil assessment, bilateral upper- and lower-limb power, sensation, and comparison with the preoperative baseline.
3. Monitor airway, voice, swallowing, neck circumference, and wound swelling closely during the first postoperative hours.
4. Escalate immediately for stridor, respiratory distress, rapidly increasing neck swelling, severe dysphagia, voice deterioration, or suspected expanding haematoma.
5. Continue prescribed multimodal analgesia and reassess pain regularly, aiming for adequate comfort while avoiding excessive sedation.
6. Maintain the wound dressing and inspect it for bleeding, discharge, swelling, erythema, or signs of infection.
7. Measure and document drain output regularly. Notify the neurosurgical team of sudden increased output, fresh blood, or failure of the drain to function.
8. Administer antiemetics as prescribed and prevent vomiting or excessive coughing where possible.
9. Maintain intravenous fluids until oral intake is adequate, then encourage oral fluids as tolerated.
10. Assess swallowing before advancing the diet; begin with clear fluids and progress as tolerated.
11. Mobilise progressively with assistance once fully awake and haemodynamically stable. Encourage safe ambulation and avoid neck hyperextension, heavy lifting, and sudden twisting.
12. Apply mechanical thromboprophylaxis and commence pharmacological thromboprophylaxis only according to the surgeon’s prescription and bleeding-risk assessment.
13. Review postoperative cervical spine radiographs to confirm alignment and satisfactory cage, plate, and screw position.
14. Monitor urine output and confirm spontaneous voiding before discharge from the ward.
15. Escalate urgently for new limb weakness, progressive sensory loss, loss of coordination, severe recurrent radicular pain, new bladder or bowel dysfunction, fever, wound discharge, or altered consciousness.
16. Before discharge, provide instructions regarding wound care, activity restrictions, medication, warning symptoms, follow-up with neurosurgery, and review of postoperative imaging.

* Age: 28 years.

R — Recommendation

1. Continue regular postoperative observations and vital-sign monitoring according to the spinal unit protocol.
2. Perform neurological observations at the prescribed frequency, including bilateral lower-limb motor power, sensation, reflexes, saddle sensation, and bladder/bowel function.

13. Postoperative diagnosis: L4–L5 prolapsed intervertebral disc with left-sided nerve-root compression and segmental instability
Current condition: Haemodynamically stable, awake, oriented, and neurologically intact

S — Situation

A 28-year-old patient is postoperative day 1 following L4–L5 lumbar discectomy, decompression, and posterior spinal fixation for a prolapsed intervertebral disc causing left-sided radiculopathy and segmental instability.

The patient is currently haemodynamically stable, awake, and oriented. Bilateral lower-limb motor power is preserved, with no new sensory deficit or sphincter disturbance. The surgical dressing is clean and dry, and pain is controlled with prescribed analgesia.

The immediate priorities are continued neurological monitoring, pain management, wound and drain assessment, prevention of postoperative complications, and progressive mobilisation with physiotherapy.

P — Patient Background

* Age: 28 years.
* Primary diagnosis: L4–L5 prolapsed intervertebral disc with left L5 nerve-root compression and segmental instability.
* Procedure performed: L4–L5 lumbar discectomy and decompression with posterior pedicle-screw fixation and interbody fusion.
* Operated level: L4–L5.
* Presenting symptoms: Six-month history of low-back pain radiating to the left buttock and lateral leg, associated with numbness over the dorsum of the left foot and intermittent weakness of great-toe extension. Symptoms were aggravated by standing, walking, and coughing.
* Relevant medical history: No significant chronic medical conditions. No history of diabetes, hypertension, cardiac disease, or bleeding disorder.
* Allergies: No known drug allergies.
* Regular medications: No regular long-term medications. Preoperative nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs were withheld before surgery.
* Previous surgical history: No previous spinal surgery. Previous surgical history otherwise unremarkable.
* Preoperative neurological status: Left ankle dorsiflexion and great-toe extension were mildly reduced at 4/5. Right lower-limb power was 5/5. There was reduced sensation over the left L5 dermatome. No saddle anaesthesia or bowel/bladder dysfunction was reported.
* Preoperative imaging: MRI demonstrated a large left paracentral L4–L5 disc extrusion with compression of the traversing left L5 nerve root, associated with degenerative disc changes and segmental instability.
* Intraoperative course: Procedure completed without reported intraoperative complications. Neural structures were decompressed satisfactorily, and fixation was placed under fluoroscopic guidance.
* Estimated blood loss: Approximately 150 mL.
* Drains: One closed-suction wound drain in situ, with minimal serosanguineous output.
* Antibiotics: Perioperative intravenous cefazolin administered according to protocol.
* Thromboprophylaxis: Mechanical prophylaxis with intermittent pneumatic compression devices; pharmacological prophylaxis to commence according to the spinal team’s postoperative plan.

A — Assessment

1. General condition

* General condition: Comfortable at rest and haemodynamically stable.
* Airway and breathing: Airway patent; breathing spontaneous and unlaboured; chest expansion symmetrical.
* Blood pressure: 118/72 mmHg.
* Heart rate: 78 beats/min.
* Respiratory rate: 16 breaths/min.
* Oxygen saturation: 98% on room air.
* Temperature: 36.8 °C.
* Pain score: 3/10 at rest and 5/10 on movement.
* Pain control: Adequate with regular paracetamol and prescribed opioid analgesia as required.
* Nausea and vomiting: No nausea or vomiting reported.
* GCS: 15/15.
* Consciousness and orientation: Awake, alert, and oriented to person, place, and time.

2. Neurological assessment

* Right lower-limb motor power:
    * Hip flexion: 5/5.
    * Knee extension: 5/5.
    * Ankle dorsiflexion: 5/5.
    * Great-toe extension: 5/5.
    * Plantarflexion: 5/5.
* Left lower-limb motor power:
    * Hip flexion: 5/5.
    * Knee extension: 5/5.
    * Ankle dorsiflexion: 5/5.
    * Great-toe extension: 5/5.
    * Plantarflexion: 5/5.
* Sensation: Light-touch sensation intact bilaterally in the lower limbs. Previous left L5-distribution numbness has improved, with mild residual altered sensation over the dorsum of the left foot.
* Deep tendon reflexes: Patellar reflexes 2+ and symmetrical; Achilles reflexes 2+ and symmetrical. No pathological reflexes elicited.
* Saddle sensation: Intact.
* Bladder and bowel function: Foley catheter removed this morning. Patient has passed urine spontaneously without retention. No new bowel dysfunction reported.
* Radicular symptoms: Preoperative left leg pain has significantly improved. No new radicular pain reported.
* Comparison with preoperative status: Motor power has improved from 4/5 to 5/5 in left ankle dorsiflexion and great-toe extension. Sensory symptoms are improved. No new neurological deficit identified.

3. Surgical site and postoperative recovery

* Wound dressing: Clean, dry, and intact, with no visible bleeding or soakage.
* Surgical wound: No erythema, swelling, wound separation, or purulent discharge.
* Drain output: Approximately 30 mL of serosanguineous fluid over the last 8 hours; no sudden increase in output.
* Pain control: Adequate on the current analgesic regimen.
* Mobilisation: Sat out of bed with assistance and mobilised approximately 20 metres with physiotherapy. No dizziness or new neurological symptoms during mobilisation.
* Spinal precautions: Avoiding heavy lifting, excessive bending, and twisting. Lumbar brace to be used when mobilising, as prescribed.
* Urine output and fluid balance: Urine output approximately 55–70 mL/hour. Fluid balance satisfactory.
* Oral intake: Tolerating oral fluids and a light diet. No nausea or vomiting.
* Bowel function: Passing flatus; no abdominal distension. Bowel regimen commenced because of opioid use.
* Laboratory results:
    * Haemoglobin: 12.8 g/dL.
    * White-cell count: 9.4 × 10⁹/L.
    * Platelets: 248 × 10⁹/L.
    * Creatinine: 78 µmol/L.
    * Electrolytes within normal limits.
* Postoperative imaging: Lumbar spine radiographs demonstrate satisfactory alignment and appropriate position of the fixation screws and interbody device, with no acute hardware complication.

4. Clinical impression

A 28-year-old patient on postoperative day 1 following L4–L5 lumbar discectomy, decompression, and posterior spinal fixation for a left paracentral disc extrusion with L5 nerve-root compression and segmental instability.

The patient is haemodynamically stable, alert, and neurologically intact. Preoperative left-sided radicular pain and mild motor weakness have improved. The wound is clean and dry, drain output is minimal and serosanguineous, pain is adequately controlled, and mobilisation has commenced safely.

R — Recommendation

1. Continue regular postoperative observations and vital-sign monitoring according to the spinal unit protocol.
2. Perform neurological observations at the prescribed frequency, including bilateral lower-limb motor power, sensation, reflexes, saddle sensation, and bladder/bowel function.
3. Compare each neurological assessment with the documented preoperative and immediate postoperative baseline.
4. Continue prescribed multimodal analgesia, including regular paracetamol and opioid analgesia only as required. Monitor for sedation, respiratory depression, nausea, and constipation.
5. Maintain the wound dressing and inspect it regularly for bleeding, soakage, swelling, erythema, discharge, or wound separation.
6. Continue monitoring the closed-suction drain and document the volume and character of output. Discuss removal with the spinal team when output is appropriately low.
7. Continue mobilisation with physiotherapy. Encourage sitting out of bed and progressive walking as tolerated.
8. Maintain spinal precautions, including avoidance of heavy lifting, excessive bending, and twisting. Use the lumbar brace during mobilisation if prescribed.
9. Continue mechanical thromboprophylaxis and commence pharmacological thromboprophylaxis only according to the spinal surgeon’s plan and local protocol.
10. Monitor urine output and assess for urinary retention following catheter removal.
11. Continue oral fluids and advance diet as tolerated. Maintain the prescribed bowel regimen while opioids are being used.
12. Review postoperative blood results and repeat investigations only if clinically indicated or if there is concern regarding bleeding, infection, or other complications.
13. Escalate immediately to the spinal surgical team for new or progressive lower-limb weakness, worsening sensory loss, saddle anaesthesia, new urinary retention, bowel incontinence, severe recurrent radicular pain, rapidly increasing drain output, wound swelling, fever with clinical deterioration, or uncontrolled pain.
14. Confirm that postoperative imaging has been reviewed and that implant alignment is satisfactory.
15. Before discharge, confirm stable neurological findings, independent or safely assisted mobilisation, adequate oral intake, satisfactory pain control, spontaneous urination, acceptable wound condition, and a clear bowel regimen.
16. Provide discharge education regarding wound care, activity restrictions, warning symptoms, medication use, and when to seek urgent medical attention.
17. Arrange follow-up with the spinal surgery clinic in approximately 2–6 weeks, with earlier review if symptoms worsen.

Patient: 50-year-old patient
Diagnosis: Lumbar spinal cord/cauda equina region tumour
Procedure: Lumbar spinal tumour resection
Current condition: Haemodynamically stable, alert, and neurologically intact postoperatively

S — Situation

A 50-year-old patient underwent elective resection of a lumbar spinal tumour at the L2–L3 level. The procedure was completed without reported intraoperative complications. The patient is currently awake, haemodynamically stable, and maintaining oxygen saturation on room air. Bilateral lower-limb motor function is preserved, with no new postoperative neurological deficit identified.

The immediate priorities are continued neurological observation, pain control, wound and drain monitoring, assessment of bladder and bowel function, prevention of postoperative complications, and review of histopathology to guide further treatment.

P — Patient Background

* Age: 50 years.
* Primary diagnosis: Intradural extramedullary tumour involving the lumbar canal and cauda equina region, centred at L2–L3.
* Surgical procedure: L2–L3 laminectomy with microsurgical resection of the lumbar spinal tumour.
* Presenting symptoms: Six-month history of progressive lower-back pain with bilateral radicular pain, worse on the right, associated with intermittent paraesthesia in the feet. No preoperative bowel or bladder incontinence was reported.
* Preoperative imaging: MRI demonstrated an enhancing intradural extramedullary mass at L2–L3 causing compression and displacement of the cauda equina nerve roots.
* Preoperative neurological status: Patient was alert and oriented. Lower-limb power was 5/5 bilaterally, with mild reduction in sensation over the right L4 dermatome. Gait was mildly antalgic. Bladder and bowel function were intact.
* Relevant medical history: Hypertension controlled with amlodipine. No diabetes mellitus or known bleeding disorder.
* Regular medications: Amlodipine 5 mg orally once daily. No regular anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy.
* Allergies: No known drug allergies.
* Intraoperative course: Tumour was removed using microsurgical technique with intraoperative neuromonitoring. No significant blood loss or neurological deterioration was reported. A small suction drain was placed.
* Histopathology: Specimen sent for histopathological examination; final diagnosis is pending.
* Postoperative imaging: MRI of the lumbar spine with contrast is planned within 24–48 hours, according to the neurosurgical team’s protocol, to assess the extent of resection and exclude significant residual tumour.

A — Assessment

1. General condition and observations

* General condition: Comfortable, awake, and haemodynamically stable.
* Airway and breathing: Airway patent; breathing spontaneous and unlaboured.
* Blood pressure: 132/78 mmHg.
* Heart rate: 78 beats/minute, regular.
* Respiratory rate: 16 breaths/minute.
* Oxygen saturation: 98% on room air.
* Temperature: 36.8°C.
* Pain score: 4/10 at the operative site, improved after prescribed analgesia.
* Level of consciousness: GCS 15/15; alert and oriented to person, place, and time.
* Fluid balance: Adequate urine output, approximately 45–60 mL/hour.
* Postoperative laboratory results: Haemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, white-cell count 9.4 × 10⁹/L, platelets 238 × 10⁹/L, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL.

2. Neurological assessment

* Motor function: Preserved bilaterally with no new weakness.
* Right lower limb: Hip flexion 5/5, knee extension 5/5, ankle dorsiflexion 5/5, great-toe extension 5/5, and plantarflexion 5/5.
* Left lower limb: Hip flexion 5/5, knee extension 5/5, ankle dorsiflexion 5/5, great-toe extension 5/5, and plantarflexion 5/5.
* Upper-limb power: 5/5 bilaterally.
* Sensory examination: Mild pre-existing reduction in sensation over the right L4 distribution; no new sensory loss, saddle anaesthesia, or ascending numbness.
* Reflexes: Patellar and Achilles reflexes present and symmetrical. No new pathological reflexes identified.
* Gait and mobility: Not yet independently assessed because the patient remains in the immediate postoperative period. Mobilisation with assistance is planned once cleared by the neurosurgical team.
* Bladder function: Indwelling urinary catheter remains in place for monitoring. Urine is clear, with adequate output. No evidence of urinary retention.
* Bowel function: No new bowel dysfunction reported. Abdomen soft and non-distended.
* Comparison with baseline: Postoperative neurological examination is unchanged from or slightly improved compared with the preoperative baseline, with preserved motor function and no new sphincter disturbance.

3. Surgical site and postoperative recovery

* Wound dressing: Clean, dry, and intact.
* Surgical wound: No active bleeding, excessive swelling, erythema, or purulent discharge.
* Drain: One lumbar suction drain in situ, producing approximately 35 mL of serosanguineous fluid over the last 8 hours.
* Pain control: Pain is adequately controlled with prescribed multimodal analgesia. No excessive sedation or respiratory depression observed.
* Fluid balance and urine output: Adequate urine output with balanced fluid status.
* Mobilisation: Bed rest maintained initially as prescribed. Patient may sit out of bed and mobilise with assistance after review by the neurosurgical team.

### SBAR Postoperative Handover

S – Situation

* 44-year-old female patient admitted with chronic calculous cholecystitis.

* Underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

* Postoperative day 0; vitally stable.

B – Background

* Admitted for surgical management of chronic calculous cholecystitis.

* Currently NPO with a nasogastric tube in place.

A – Assessment

* Patient is alert and vitally stable.

* Abdomen is non-tender, with average bowel sounds.

* Has not passed stool yet.

* Drain output is approximately 50 mL of serosanguineous fluid.

R – Recommendation / Plan

* Remove the nasogastric tube and start oral fluids at 1:00 a.m., as planned.

* Gradually advance the diet according to tolerance and the treating team's instructions.

* Monitor vital signs, abdominal examination, bowel function, and drain output.

* Consider discharge once the patient is clinically stable and tolerating a full diet, according to the surgical team's assessment.

# Situation:
* Case of AKI (Acute Kidney Injury), chest infection, systemic congestion, and chronic lower limb (LL) ischemia.

# Background:

* Past Medical History (PMHx): Hypertension (HTN), Diabetes Mellitus (DM), and Ischemic Heart Disease (IHD) post-PCI (Percutaneous Coronary Intervention) with stent insertion, Contrast induced nephropathy .

## Assessment

* CNS: Confusion.
* CVS: Hemodynamically stable.
* Chest: : still on NC 1 L sat 92 % abg show chronic respiratory acidosis.
* Abdomen: Lax, distended, and patient has passed stool soft consistency
* lacteol fort added 
* C diff in stool requested 
* No fever 
ultrasound show gradual resolve of pelvic hematoma

## Recommendation
- Vital signs monitoring
fluid chart and Balance
- follow up ultrasound 
- Negative balance

Situation
Tinged blood in foley >> traumatic for urology consultation 
Patient didn’t pass stool >> General surgery consultation
- Persistent bilateral lower-limb edema with mildly decreased air entry. 

Background 

Patient has spinal cord lesion with atony, contributing to constipation.
- General Surgery reviewed the patient and prescribed medication for constipation.
- Grade 2 bed sores were examined by General Surgery.

Assessment 

Maintaining good urine output,
- CRP is decreasing on follow up 
- Blood culture and wound swab culture showed no growth.
- Urine culture showed MDR 
- Persistent LL edema and mildly decreased air entry.
-Pelvis US done showing no blood clots inside the bladder despite hematuria ( will hold anti coagulant temporarily )

Recommendations

Follow up temperature curve and inflammatory markers and electrolytes 
Continue monitoring fluid balance, urine output, respiratory status, and edema.
Added meronem and adjust all doses according CrCl
Dc Nahco3 
GIT and urology consultations Done

### SPAR Clinical Summary – Oncology Ward Round

S – Situation

* 50-year-old male, no known comorbidities.

* Diagnosed with metastatic colorectal cancer.

* Last chemotherapy: Capecitabine (Xeloda; 9 days on/5 days off as reported) + targeted therapy.

* Recent cystoscopy 10 days ago for hematuria.

* Admitted to ICU following convulsions, with suspected meningitis.

P – Problem

* Fever and headache on presentation.

* Bilateral lower limb weakness.

* Convulsions.

* Suspected meningitis/CNS infection.

* Hematuria following recent cystoscopy — current status needs confirmation.

A – Assessment (Update: 13/10)

* Afebrile currently.

* Persistent headache and bilateral lower limb weakness.

* Hematuria: status unclear.

* Laboratory results reported as acceptable.

* Receiving empirical antimicrobial/antiviral treatment and corticosteroids for suspected CNS infection/inflammation.

R – Recommendation

* Continue close neurological monitoring; document GCS, power in both lower limbs, and any recurrent seizures.

* Review brain imaging (MRI preferred when feasible) and CSF results if lumbar puncture is safe; exclude intracranial metastases, cerebral edema, and other causes of neurological deterioration.

* Review cultures and reassess the need for meropenem, vancomycin, and acyclovir according to results and clinical response.

* Continue levetiracetam (Tiratam) and dexamethasone as clinically indicated; reassess ongoing indications.

* Clarify hematuria status; monitor urine output, CBC, renal function, and coagulation profile, with urology review if persistent.

* Reassess systemic anticancer treatment during the acute illness.

S – Situation:
55-year-old female patient diagnosed with metastatic ovarian cancer, status post total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TAHBSO) and hemicolectomy. The patient was admitted due to sepsis and is currently receiving supportive treatment. Current laboratory investigations indicate persistent sepsis and acute kidney injury (AKI). She is also experiencing hypokalemia and is receiving potassium correction.
B – Background:
History of double-J (DJ) stent placement.
History of left lower-limb DVT, status post IVC filter placement.
Undergoing chest physiotherapy and right-sided physiotherapy.
Previous hematuria, which has now resolved.
IVC assessment revealed a diameter of 22 mm with reduced collapsibility.
A – Assessment:
Sepsis with associated acute kidney injury (AKI).
Hypokalemia on potassium replacement therapy.
IVC assessment suggests elevated right atrial pressure; fluid status should be correlated with the clinical examination and hemodynamic parameters.
New complaint of ear pain and tinnitus.
Hematuria has stopped.
Close blood pressure monitoring is recommended.
Currently receiving supportive treatment.
R – Recommendation:
Continue supportive treatment and management of sepsis and AKI.
Continue potassium correction with follow-up electrolyte monitoring.
Closely monitor blood pressure, vital signs, urine output, and renal function.
Monitor fluid balance carefully in view of AKI and the IVC assessment findings.
Arrange ENT consultation for ear pain and tinnitus.
Repeat laboratory investigations tomorrow to reassess renal function, electrolytes, and inflammatory markers.
Continue chest and right-sided physiotherapy as clinically indicated.
Monitor for recurrence of hematuria.

### SPAR Clinical Summary – Oncology Ward Round

S – Situation

* 14-year-old male diagnosed with osteosarcoma.

* Receiving chemotherapy, including methotrexate.

* On gastric supportive treatment following chemotherapy due to vomiting and diarrhea.

P – Problem

* Chemotherapy-related gastrointestinal symptoms: vomiting and diarrhea.

* Shoulder pain requiring analgesia.

A – Assessment (Current Update)

* Patient is still receiving chemotherapy.

* Shoulder pain managed with Panadol (paracetamol); reassessment of pain response is needed.

* Current severity of vomiting and diarrhea is not specified.

R – Recommendation

* Monitor vital signs regularly, including temperature and hydration status.

* Assess vomiting and diarrhea, oral intake, urine output, and signs of dehydration.

* Check CBC, renal function, and electrolytes as clinically indicated, particularly during methotrexate treatment.

* Assess shoulder pain severity, location, and response to paracetamol; investigate persistent or worsening pain as indicated.

* Ensure methotrexate toxicity monitoring and confirm appropriate supportive care, including hydration, leucovorin rescue, and methotrexate level monitoring when required by the protocol.

Plan: Follow up vital signs, gastrointestinal symptoms, hydration, and shoulder pain.
